64.title: The Evolutionary Races of Color
64.b0.ask: “How were the six colored races born of a single family among the descendants of Andon, and how did they spread over all the earth?”
64.b2.p: In Paper 63 we saw the family of Andon and Fonta grow into clans and reach the golden age of primitive man under Onagar. Paper 64 continues the story of the evolutionary races over almost one million years — from the days of Andon and Fonta, through the times of the Planetary Prince, to the end of the ice age.
64.b3.p: The first half of human history roughly corresponds to the days before the Planetary Prince. The second half begins with the arrival of the Planetary Prince and the appearance of the six colored races, and roughly matches what is commonly called the Old Stone Age.
64.b4.p: What rises and falls, then, did the descendants of Andon pass through? And where and how did the six colored races appear, and what paths did they take?
64.b5.q: ⟦Q 64:6.27⟧Notwithstanding their backwardness, these indigo peoples have exactly the same standing before the celestial powers as any other earthly race.⟦/Q⟧
64.b8.p: Early man was hemmed in: by the high Tibetan lands to the east, by the Mediterranean, which then reached to the Indian Ocean, to the south and west, and by the advancing ice to the north. Mountains to the right, water to the left, and ice in front — many of man’s earliest religious feelings grew out of this helplessness. Yet the progressive Andonites would not turn back to their tree-dwelling relatives in the south.
64.b9.p: The Andonites avoided the forests. In the forests man has always deteriorated; human evolution has progressed only in the open and in the higher latitudes, where cold and hunger stimulate action, invention, and resourcefulness. By 950,000 years ago they had spread west to France and England and east as far as Java and Tasmania. But the groups going east mingled with their inferior cousins, fewer and fewer settlements kept up the worship of the Breath Giver, and the dawn civilization was threatened with extinction.
64.b10.t: The Tibetan highlands, 30,000 feet above sea level
The Mediterranean, reaching to the Indian Ocean
64.b12.p: By 900,000 years ago the arts of Andon and Fonta and the culture of Onagar were vanishing; culture, religion, and even flintworking were at their lowest ebb. In southern France mixed groups that could hardly be called human pressed into England, and later the Heidelberg race spread over Europe.
64.b13.p: Through this long decline two groups held on to the traditions of Andon and remnants of Onagar’s culture. The Foxhall peoples of England, the first human inhabitants there, preserved the knowledge of flintworking, and the more spiritual among them later moved on west and survive as the present-day Eskimos.
64.b14.t: Farthest west, in England — kept flintworking; ancestors of the Eskimos
The highlands northwest of India — never practiced human sacrifice
64.b16.p: In the east, culture lived on in the foothills of the northwestern Indian highlands among the tribes of Badonan, a great-great-grandson of Andon. These were the only descendants of Andon who never practiced human sacrifice. While the northern tribes feared the ice, these people, who had watched the Mesopotamian peninsula sink into the ocean, feared the water, and so they lived in the highlands.
64.b17.p: About 850,000 years ago the superior Badonan tribes waged a war of extermination against their animalistic neighbors and in less than a thousand years had largely driven them out. The mixed descendants of this improved Badonite stock appeared as an apparently new people: the Neanderthal race.
64.b19.p: The Neanderthalers were excellent fighters and hunters. They spread from northwest India to France, China, and northern Africa, and dominated the world for almost half a million years, until the colored races migrated. The reindeer gave them food, clothing, and tools, and they speared fish through holes in the ice. Yet over almost a quarter of a million years they steadily retrogressed compared with their Andonic ancestors.
64.b20.t: The fourth ice sheet moved south — fishing through holes in the ice
The fourth glacier retreated — men and animals returned north
A mild interglacial — the Alps almost bare of ice
After the farthest retreat, the fifth glacier started south
Pushed south again, but with wide lands toward Asia
64.b21.p: In these spiritually dark ages the Neanderthalers had no religion beyond a shameful superstition. They were deathly afraid of clouds, mists, fogs, and darkness, and their religion of fear led to the sacrifice of human beings to appease unseen forces. In the dark of the moon they sacrificed their finest men and women to make the moon shine again.
64.b23.p: Five hundred thousand years ago a racial war of more than a hundred years broke out among the Badonan tribes, leaving only about one hundred families. But these survivors were the most intelligent of all Andon’s living descendants. Then a man and woman in the northeastern part of the highlands suddenly began to produce unusually intelligent children. This was the Sangik family, the ancestors of all six colored races.
64.b24.p: The nineteen Sangik children had skins that turned various colors in sunlight, and the colors grew stronger as they grew older. When they mated within the tribe, all their offspring tended toward the skin color of the Sangik parent. It was at about this time that the Planetary Prince arrived.
64.b26.h: 6. The Six Sangik Races of Urantia
64.b27.p: On an average evolutionary world the six colored races appear one by one, beginning with the red man. The appearance of all six at once, and in one family, as on Urantia, was most unusual. The evolution of the Andonites before the colored races was also something new in the Satania system.
64.b28.t: The most advanced; first tribal government; monogamy
An urge to build; vast heaps of stone
First farming settlements; brotherhood and co-operation
Invented the spear; the red man’s brain with the yellow man’s soul
The least advanced; settled in Africa
64.b29.p: The red men, driven off by the yellow tribes, crossed into North America about 85,000 years ago but declined through tribal wars. The yellow race survived in the largest numbers because of its peaceful ways. The blue men were the Adamic descendants’ favorite among the colored races, and the so-called white races are their descendants, greatly upstepped by assimilating the violet race. The indigo race was the least advanced, yet it has exactly the same standing before the celestial powers as any other race.
64.b30.p: There are good and sufficient reasons for evolving three or six colored races on a world. Although mortals may not fully appreciate them all, the book points out five.
64.b31.t: Opportunity for the wide working of natural selection
Stronger and better races can result
Essential to the growth of tolerance and altruism
Not desirable until high spiritual levels are reached
64.b33.p: As the Sangik descendants multiplied, the fifth glacier spread far and cut off the road to eastern Asia, and for a long time they lived mixed together in the foothills. The superior primary Sangik races avoided the tropics and went north, while the secondary Sangik races were drawn to the easier southlands.
64.b34.p: A little over seven thousand of the red race left Asia for North America, and the mixed groups that went with them founded the civilizations of Mexico, Central America, and South America. The blue men entered Europe, mingled with the Neanderthalers, and improved them. Egypt was ruled in turn by the orange, the green, and the indigo races.
64.b35.t: A mixture of the secondary Sangik races
The brown race (a blend of red and yellow)
The islands off the Asiatic coast
The far north of Europe, Iceland, Greenland, and northeastern North America
64.b36.p: The westernmost Andon tribes, driven by the glaciers, built boats and became the first marine adventurers, and their Eskimo descendants later crossed into North America. The Life Carrier regrets that so many of the rugged traits of our early ancestors have been lost to later races.
64.b37.q: ⟦Q 64:7.20⟧While we appreciate the value of many of the refinements of advancing civilization, we miss the magnificent persistency and superb devotion of your early ancestors, which oftentimes bordered on grandeur and sublimity.⟦/Q⟧
64.b39.p: Paper 64 traces almost a million years of human rise and fall as one continuous story. The descendants of Andon held out between glaciers, mountains, and sea, and at times slipped backward, while small groups such as the Foxhall peoples and the Badonites kept the old traditions alive. Then, in the Badonan highlands, the Sangik family gave birth to all six colored races at once, and they scattered over every continent with the movements of the ice. Each race rose and declined for its own reasons, yet every race had teachers who brought spiritual revival, and all races stand equal before the celestial powers. The courage and devotion of our ancestors are written into this long struggle.
64.b40.t: Hemmed in by mountains, water, and ice, man progressed only in the open
Through the long decline, Andon’s culture was kept alive in the far west
From highland tribes who never sacrificed humans came the Neanderthalers
They ruled for half a million years but declined in a religion of fear
The nineteen Sangik children showed six skin colors
6. The Six Sangik Races of Urantia
Six races born at once in one family was most unusual
Scattered by the glaciers, the races formed today’s pattern on the continents
64.b42.box: The six colored races were born of one family, and though their paths differ, all have the same standing before the celestial powers.
65.title: The Overcontrol of Evolution
65.b0.ask: “Behind the evolution of life, which can look like a string of accidents, who is guiding the way, and how does that guidance carry a purpose?”
65.b2.p: In Paper 64 we followed the long story of the Andon descendants and the six colored races as they spread across the earth in the wake of the glaciers. Now Paper 65 steps back to look at the hands that guided all of that evolution. Basic material life is the work of three agencies acting together: the formulation of the Master Physical Controllers, the life-impartation ministry of the Seven Master Spirits, and the active ministration of the Life Carriers.
65.b3.p: Life production and evolution unfold on three levels. The mechanical, nonteachable responses of organisms belong to the physical controllers. The kind of mind that can learn from experience is activated by the adjutant spirits. And the Life Carriers guide the environmental conditions right up to the appearance of human will. Because these three work as one, evolution is always purposeful and never accidental.
65.b4.p: How, then, do the Life Carriers work? What twists and turns has evolution taken? And where do mind and spirit fit into the process?
65.b5.q: ⟦Q 65:8.5⟧If the individual really knows God and desires to find him and become like him, then survival is assured regardless of the handicaps of time.⟦/Q⟧
65.b8.p: The Life Carriers have been given a power of personality transformation that only a few orders of creatures possess. Ordinarily they work as mid-phase Sons, the state of their origin. But in that state they cannot join physical energies and material particles into units of living existence. So when they are ready to plant life, an archangel commission transmutes them to the physical level of electrochemistry. As soon as life appears, they are returned at once to their normal mid-phase.
65.b9.t: Organize and create new patterns of living matter
2. The usual mid-phase of quasi-morontial existence
Manipulate the living units and guide the evolving organisms
After the renunciation vows, serve as advisers to the new will creatures
Hoped for when the universe is settled in light and life
65.b10.p: Once free will of the human type appears, the Life Carriers must either leave the planet or take renunciation vows, pledging never again to try to influence the course of organic evolution. Those who choose to stay are transmuted to the semispiritual level. The author of this paper has served on Urantia in that third phase ever since the times of Andon and Fonta.
65.b12.p: The story of man's ascent from seaweed to the lordship of earthly creation is a romance of biologic struggle and mind survival. Our primordial ancestors were literally the slime and ooze of the ocean bed in the warm bays and lagoons of the ancient inland seas, where the Life Carriers established three independent life implantations. Borderline organisms much like sponges opened the way from plant to animal. Bacteria and the ameba are survivors of those first steps that failed to develop further.
65.b13.t: Spongelike forms opened the way to true animals
Volvox, Hydra, jellyfish, mollusks, and many more
The start of the differentiations that led to man
Source of the birds and the many orders of mammals
Probably the greatest single leap of prehuman evolution
A small carnivorous dinosaur → placental mammals
Branching even into whales, seals, and bats
65.b14.p: The frog is the only living species ancestor of the human race; between the frog and the Eskimo, mankind has no surviving ancestry. Man evolved from higher mammals that came mainly from the western implantation of life. The eastern group lost its human potential through repeated losses of its best germ plasm. Nor was it an accident that primitive man appeared during the ice age. It was by design, meant to produce a hardy human type with great power to survive.
65.b16.p: The Life Carriers may use every natural resource and every fortunate circumstance, but they are not allowed to intervene mechanically in evolution or to manipulate it arbitrarily. Our ancestral frog once came close to extinction, yet even then the Life Carriers were fostering at least a thousand other strains of life. That frog was their third choice; the two earlier strains had perished despite all their efforts. Even if Andon and Fonta had died without children, human evolution would have been delayed, not prevented.
65.b17.p: No more races will now arise from prehuman sources. Still, by wisely fostering the potentials that remain in the mortal races, mankind can reach far higher levels of development. What the Life Carriers did before the appearance of will, man must now do for himself. His evolutionary destiny is largely in his own hands.
65.b18.q: ⟦Q 65:3.6⟧In a general way, man's evolutionary destiny is in his own hands, and scientific intelligence must sooner or later supersede the random functioning of uncontrolled natural selection and chance survival.⟦/Q⟧
65.b20.p: Urantia was a life-experiment world, the sixtieth attempt to improve the Satania adaptation of the Nebadon life designs. Here the Life Carriers worked out at least twenty-eight life modifications that will serve all Nebadon in the future. Yet the experiment was not a gamble. The evolution of life is a technique ever progressive and variable, but never haphazard.
65.b21.p: The healing of wounds shows how carefully life was planned. An injured cell releases chemicals that stir the neighboring cells to secrete healing substances and to make new cells. To choose this formula from more than one hundred thousand possible features, the Life Carriers made over half a million experiments. Here is what made the Urantia experiment unique:
65.b22.t: In the colored races, usually the red man
In a precolored race, the Andonites
Appear one at a time over long ages
All six sprang from a single family
Almost five hundred thousand years later
65.b23.p: To obtain the needed combination of inheritance factors, the Life Carriers had to allow thousands of other, comparatively useless combinations. These strange by-products may well puzzle those who dig back into the planet's past.
65.b25.p: The work of the Life Carriers was badly handicapped by tragedies beyond their control: the Caligastia betrayal and the Adamic default. Their greatest disappointment was the reversion of certain primitive plants to parasitic bacteria, which brought many diseases on man. They had expected that the Adamic life plasm, once blended in, would make the race practically immune to such diseases, but that hope was lost through the Adamic default.
65.b26.p: Even so, the universe is not run to please us or to satisfy our curiosity. The wise beings who manage it know exactly what they are about, so both Life Carriers and mortals do well to wait patiently and co-operate wholeheartedly. There are compensations too, such as Michael's bestowal on Urantia, and the celestial supervisors of this planet are fully confident of the ultimate evolutionary triumph of the human race.
65.b28.p: The scientist will come nearer and nearer to the secrets of life, but he will never find them, because he must kill protoplasm in order to analyze it. Dead protoplasm weighs the same as living protoplasm, but it is not the same. Every living thing carries an insatiable craving for better adaptation, an innate striving for perfection.
65.b29.t: Chlorophyll-making ability; the spore becoming the seed
Man uses iron, the cuttlefish copper, the sea squirt vanadium
Over 15,000,000 possible reactions among hormones in the blood
65.b30.p: But physics and chemistry alone cannot explain how man evolved. The laws of physics do not respond to training and chemical reactions are not changed by education, but mind learns from experience. Preintelligent organisms only react to their surroundings, while organisms that respond to mind ministry can change the environment itself.
65.b32.p: The seven adjutant mind-spirits are the mind ministers to the lower intelligent beings of a local universe, more circuitlike than entitylike. They take no part in physical evolution, which is the domain of the Life Carriers. Yet their work is so perfectly woven into natural processes that mortals see in the phenomenon of mind nothing but the hand of nature. On Urantia, because of its unusual life patterns, the adjutants had almost the greatest difficulty they had ever met anywhere in Nebadon in making contact with evolving minds.
65.b33.t: The power centers and physical controllers
Still additional spirit ministry accompanies it
65.b34.p: In the ministry of the spirit world there are no abrupt transitions; all changes are gradual and reciprocal. The physical, the mental, and the spiritual are closely related, yet they remain distinct realms of cosmic reality.
65.b36.p: Evolution takes so long because the Life Carriers cannot make life unfold faster than the physical changes of the planet allow. If conditions permitted, they could complete it in much less than a million years. Creatures measure time by the length of their own lives, so evolution seems slow to them. But on Paradise time does not exist; all these things are simply present.
65.b37.p: Spiritual progress depends on the growth of mind, so it can be held back by intellectual slowness. Yet the soul can evolve regardless of mental culture, though not without the choice to survive and the decision to do the will of the Father. Survival may not depend on knowledge and wisdom, but progress certainly does. The body may hinder the mind and the mind may delay the spirit, yet none of these obstacles can defeat the whole-souled choice of will.
65.b38.t: The expansion of mind, knowledge, and wisdom
The sincere choice to know God, find him, and become like him
65.b40.p: Paper 65 bears witness, in the voice of a Life Carrier, that evolution is not a chain of accidents. The physical controllers, the adjutant spirits, and the Life Carriers work together. They fostered a thousand strains and made half a million experiments, yet never interfered arbitrarily. Betrayal and default upset their plans, but those who rule the universe know what they are doing, and the final triumph of mankind is sure. Now that the Life Carriers have stepped back, our evolutionary destiny has been placed in our own hands. And however slowly body and mind may grow, no barrier of time can stop the choice of a soul that sincerely seeks God.
65.b41.t: The Life Carriers change their phase of being to plant and tend life
From ocean ooze through the frog to man, the way was planned
Life is fostered, not forced; now man's destiny is in his own hands
On this life-experiment world, will appeared in a precolored race
Despite betrayal and default, patient co-operation leads to final triumph
Beyond physics and chemistry, mind learns and changes its surroundings
The adjutants minister gradually, beginning with mind that can learn
No obstacle can defeat the soul's choice to seek God
65.b43.box: Evolution always has a purpose, and at its end our destiny rests on our own choice to seek God.
66.title: The Planetary Prince of Urantia
66.b0.ask: “How did the Planetary Prince and his staff teach primitive mankind, and why did so brilliant a Prince fall?”
66.b2.p: In Paper 65 we saw how the Life Carriers guided evolution with purpose and then stepped back once human will appeared. Paper 66 turns to the next stage: the rule of the Planetary Prince. On an average world the coming of a Lanonandek Son means that will, the ability to choose the path of eternal survival, has developed in the mind of primitive man. But on Urantia the Planetary Prince arrived almost half a million years after the appearance of human will.
66.b3.p: Caligastia arrived about five hundred thousand years ago, at the time the six Sangik races appeared. Almost half a billion primitive human beings were then scattered over Europe, Asia, and Africa, and the Prince set up his headquarters in Mesopotamia, near the center of the world's population.
66.b4.p: How did the Prince and his one hundred awaken primitive man? And how could so promising a Prince betray his sacred trust of planetary custody?
66.b5.q: ⟦Q 66:8.6⟧The free will of man is supreme in moral affairs; even the indwelling Thought Adjuster refuses to compel man to think a single thought or to perform a single act against the choosing of man's own will.⟦/Q⟧
66.b8.p: Caligastia was a Lanonandek Son of the secondary order, experienced in the affairs of the local universe and in the management of the system of Satania. Lucifer raised him to his personal staff, where he filled five assignments of honor and trust. Caligastia sought a commission as Planetary Prince very early, but his request was refused several times before he was finally assigned to Urantia. He had a certain restlessness and a habit of disagreeing with the established order in minor matters, yet his record of loyalty and devotion was enviable.
66.b9.p: The Melchizedek who wrote this paper was present on Jerusem when Caligastia departed. No Planetary Prince ever set out with a richer preparation or better prospects, and Urantia seemed one of the most fortunate planets in all Satania. But no one then realized what was quietly happening within Caligastia's heart.
66.b10.q: ⟦Q 66:1.5⟧I did not then comprehend that Caligastia was insidiously falling in love with himself; I did not then so fully understand the subtleties of personality pride.⟦/Q⟧
66.b12.p: The Prince did not come alone. At the head of his staff was his fellow Lanonandek Daligastia, and with them came many angelic co-operators. From our point of view the most interesting group were the corporeal members of the staff, known as the Caligastia one hundred. They were chosen from more than 785,000 ascendant citizens of Jerusem who volunteered for the Urantia adventure, and each came from a different planet.
66.b13.p: For their bodies, the Life Carriers chose fifty men and fifty women of the best strains of Andon and Fonta's descendants. Guided by Thought Adjusters and seraphim, these Andonites gathered at the Prince's headquarters, and part of their life plasm was transferred into the material bodies built for the one hundred. From the arrival of the seraphic transports to the moment the volunteers became conscious, threefold beings took exactly ten days.
66.b15.p: The Prince's headquarters lay in the Persian Gulf region, in the district later known as Mesopotamia. The one great task of those ages was to turn man from a hunter into a herder, in the hope that he would later become a peace-loving, home-abiding farmer. The center of the settlement was Dalamatia, named in honor of Daligastia, a simple but beautiful city enclosed by a wall forty feet high.
66.b16.t: Ten subdivisions, each with a council headquarters mansion at its center
The temple of the unseen Father, small but three stories high
Twelve chambers grouped about the temple
Mostly one-story brick houses; the council headquarters had two stories
Superior individuals from nearby tribes were trained and sent home as teachers
66.b17.p: The one hundred continually gathered the best individuals of the surrounding tribes, trained and inspired them, and then sent them back as teachers and leaders of their own peoples.
66.b18.h: 4. Early Days of the One Hundred
66.b19.p: The arrival of the staff made a deep impression, and much later mythology grew out of garbled legends of these days. The tendency of mortals to treat them as gods was a serious obstacle, yet the one hundred, fifty men and fifty women, never used supernatural methods. Still, they were superhuman, beings of a threefold nature.
66.b20.t: The threefold nature of the one hundred
They carried Andonic life plasm and lived on a nonflesh diet
Citizens of Jerusem with souls of ascendant growth; their Adjusters were detached
The fruit of the tree of life supplied the complements of the system life currents
66.b21.p: In the thirty-third year at Dalamatia, two members of the Danite group discovered by accident that the liaison of their morontia selves produced a new being: the first primary midway creature, invisible to human beings. In time the one hundred brought into being a corps of 50,000 primary midwayers, who for ages were the whole spirit world to primitive mortals. The tree of life, sent from Edentia, grew in the courtyard of the temple of the Father. Because of it, the one hundred Andonites who had given their life plasm also lived on with the staff, century after century.
66.b23.p: The one hundred were organized into ten autonomous councils of ten members each; when councils met together, Daligastia presided. Each council lifted up one side of primitive human life.
66.b24.t: Wells and irrigation, treating skins, food storage
Better cattle, the wheel, carrier pigeons
A twenty-five-letter alphabet; the library called the house of Fad
Primitive manufacture, the salt trade, the first commercial credit
Replacing ghost fear with Creator fear; the Father's prayer
Cooking and boiling, sunlight, bathing, handshaking
Rudiments of physics and chemistry, pottery, clay sculpture
Intertribal marriage, humanizing warfare, tribal government
Court of appeals for the other nine councils
66.b25.p: The staff gave no revelation that would complicate evolution, but Hap yielded to the city dwellers' desire for worship and gave them chants and the Father's prayer. The staff also held out the promise of Adam's gift of a new race as the goal after biologic development reached its height. Yet the alphabet and much else was lost in the confusion of the rebellion.
66.b26.q: ⟦Q 66:5.15⟧We pray for the hastening of the coming of the promised uplifter, and we would do your will on this world as others do on worlds beyond.⟦/Q⟧
66.b28.p: The culture of a world is measured by its social heritage, and its growth depends on how well its people can grasp new ideas. When the one hundred arrived, the whole world was caught in the stalemate of tradition-bound mores. They proclaimed a new gospel of individual initiative, but their rule was cut short so soon that the races were never wholly freed from the slavery of custom.
66.b29.p: These wise beings did not try to transform the primitive races all at once. Foreign emissaries were sent only when a people asked for them; those who worked to uplift a tribe were always natives of that tribe; and instead of imposing superior customs, they patiently lifted up the time-tried mores of each race. Their motive was progression by evolution and not revolution by revelation.
66.b30.t: Each tribe taught by its own people
Imposing the customs of a superior race
Adding social selection to natural selection
66.b32.p: The headquarters was beautiful enough to awe primitive men, yet altogether modest, and no methods were used that did not naturally belong on Urantia. The staff lived together as fathers and mothers, and their fifty pattern homes always sheltered more than five hundred adopted children. The home as a social unit took root only after these supermen and superwomen led mankind to love and plan for their grandchildren and their grandchildren's children. Education followed the plan of an industrial school, where pupils learned by doing.
66.b33.q: ⟦Q 66:7.4⟧Savage man loves his child, but civilized man loves also his grandchild.⟦/Q⟧
66.b34.p: Hap gave the early races a moral law called the Father's Way, made up of seven commands. It was the law of Dalamatia for almost three hundred thousand years. People kept one command in mind for each day of the week, and the seven-day week itself was introduced at this time, since seven was one fourth of the twenty-eight-day lunar month.
66.b35.t: Do not fear or serve any God but the Father of all
Do not disobey the world's ruler or show disrespect to his associates
Do not lie when called before the judges
Do not kill men, women, or children
Do not steal your neighbor's goods or cattle
Do not touch your friend's wife
Do not show disrespect to your parents or the elders of the tribe
66.b36.p: Farming was never a penalty for sin. The cultivation of the soil is essential to civilization on the evolutionary worlds, and it stood at the center of the Prince's teaching for three hundred thousand years. Work with the soil is not a curse; rather is it the highest blessing to all who are thus permitted to enjoy the most human of all human activities. When the rebellion broke out, almost six thousand people lived in Dalamatia, but nearly all of its wonderful gains were wiped out in the confusion that followed.
66.b38.p: Looking back over Caligastia's long career, one feature stands out: he was ultraindividualistic. He readily sided with parties of protest and mildly resented supervision, yet until he betrayed Urantia he had always proved loyal. Both he and Lucifer had been patiently instructed and lovingly warned about their critical tendencies and their pride. But they took this help as unwarranted interference, and they judged their unselfish advisers by their own evolving selfishness.
66.b39.t: Planetary civilization progressed in a fairly normal manner
He went into darkness and was deprived of sovereign authority
He contributed to the miscarriage of the violet-race plan
His power to disturb human affairs was greatly curtailed
He was finally shorn of all authority on Urantia
He awaits the final adjudication of the Ancients of Days
66.b40.p: The doctrine of a personal devil had some basis in Caligastia's presence on the planet. But the teaching that such a devil could turn the normal human mind against its own free choice is wholly fictitious. Even before Michael came, neither Caligastia nor Daligastia could ever force a normal person to do anything against the human will.
66.b42.p: Paper 66 shows both how much good a Prince over a world could do and how deeply he could fall. The Caligastia one hundred were superhuman, yet they did not rule like gods. They dug wells, taught letters, built homes, and lifted mankind slowly, without haste. At the heart of their teaching were worship of the Father of all and the blessing of tilling the soil. But the most brilliant of Princes fell through a hidden love of self and a pride that took counsel for interference. Even so, his fall could not take away man's free will. Moral choice always remains our own.
66.b43.t: Within the most promising Prince, self-love was quietly growing
The one hundred came from Jerusem and received Andonic life plasm
A modest city around a temple became the world's center of culture
4. Early Days of the One Hundred
Superhuman yet never supernatural, the one hundred brought forth the midwayers
Ten councils raised primitive man in every area of life
They taught by evolution, not revolution; by uplift, not force
They taught the home, the Father's Way, and the blessing of the soil
The Prince fell, but man's free will could not be taken away
66.b45.box: A brilliant Prince fell through love of self, but no one can take from us our own moral choice.
67.title: The Planetary Rebellion
67.b0.ask: “When the Planetary Prince rebelled, what kept Van and Amadon unshaken to the end, and what has that sin left behind for us?”
67.b2.p: In Paper 66 we watched the Caligastia one hundred slowly lift primitive mankind at Dalamatia, until the Prince's love of self put all of it in danger. Paper 67 tells how the rebellion actually happened and what it left in its wake.
67.b3.p: The problems of human life on Urantia cannot be understood without knowing certain great epochs of the past, above all the planetary rebellion and its consequences. This upheaval did not seriously disturb organic evolution, but it markedly changed the course of social evolution and spiritual development, and it deeply affected the whole superphysical history of the planet.
67.b4.p: How did the rebellion begin? Who chose what? And can another person's sin harm our own eternal destiny?
67.b5.q: ⟦Q 67:7.5⟧Never does the sin of any being rob another of the realization of the divine right of personality survival.⟦/Q⟧
67.b8.p: Caligastia had been in charge of Urantia for three hundred thousand years when Satan, Lucifer's assistant, made one of his periodic inspection calls. He looked nothing like the caricatures of later ages; he was a Lanonandek Son of great brilliance. Satan told Caligastia of Lucifer's proposed “⟦Q 67:1.2|53:2.4|53:3.1⟧Declaration of Liberty,⟦/Q⟧” and the Prince agreed to betray the planet once the rebellion was announced.
67.b9.p: No trust in a local universe is more sacred than the one placed in a Planetary Prince, and no evil destroys personality more than betrayal of trust and disloyalty to one's confiding friends. By this deliberate sin Caligastia so distorted his personality that his mind has never since fully regained its balance. Here the paper distinguishes four degrees of wrong:
67.b10.t: A misconception or distortion of reality
A partial realization of, or maladjustment to, universe realities
A purposeful resistance to divine reality
Open and persistent defiance of recognized reality
67.b11.p: Sin chosen again and again can become habitual, and habitual sinners easily become iniquitous. Every kind of sin may be forgiven, but it is doubtful whether the established iniquiter would ever sincerely feel sorrow or accept forgiveness.
67.b13.p: One day in midwinter, Daligastia called the ten councils into extraordinary session. He announced that Caligastia was about to proclaim himself absolute sovereign of Urantia and demanded that they hand over all their powers. Van, chairman of the supreme council, branded this an act bordering on planetary rebellion and urged an appeal to Lucifer. But the answer from Jerusem commanded absolute obedience to Caligastia. In reply Van gave a memorable seven-hour address indicting all three rebels and appealed to the Most Highs of Edentia for support.
67.b14.p: Meanwhile the system circuits were cut, and Urantia was isolated. Daligastia proclaimed Caligastia “⟦Q 67:2.4⟧God of Urantia and supreme over all.⟦/Q⟧” Seraphim, cherubim, and even beings who happened to be on the planet were forced to choose between the ways of Lucifer and the will of the unseen Father. The struggle went on for more than seven years, and Edentia did not intervene until every personality had made a final decision.
67.b16.p: There was “⟦Q 67:3.1|53:5.6|53:5.7⟧war in heaven⟦/Q⟧” on Jerusem, and it spread to every planet of the system. On Urantia forty of the one hundred, including Van, refused to join the insurrection. But almost half of the administrator and transition seraphim sided with Lucifer, and 40,119 primary midwayers joined Caligastia. The loyalists lived in an unwalled settlement east of Dalamatia, guarded by loyal midwayers, and they kept possession of the tree of life.
67.b17.t: The one hundred of the corporeal staff
Almost half went over to Lucifer
Fifty-six loyal, including sixteen attendants of disloyal staff members
67.b18.p: Van's unshakable loyalty grew out of clear thinking, wise reasoning, sincere motivation, unselfish purpose, disciplined character, and the unquestioning dedication of his personality to doing the Father's will. His human associate Amadon, a descendant of Andon and Fonta, stood unmoved by Daligastia's sophistries for all seven years. Caligastia, with a maximum of intelligence and vast experience, went astray. Amadon, with a minimum of intelligence and no universe experience at all, remained steadfast.
67.b19.q: ⟦Q 67:3.9⟧Mind and spirit, when fully united, are potential for the creation of superhuman values, even morontia realities.⟦/Q⟧
67.b20.p: Only after the last personality had decided did a Most High of Edentia arrive with the emergency Melchizedeks to take authority, and the probationary era of planetary rehabilitation began.
67.b21.h: 4. The Caligastia One Hundred after Rebellion
67.b22.p: When the final roll was called, forty of the one hundred were saved, later to resume their Paradise journey from Jerusem. Each council chose differently.
67.b23.t: Fad and five members were saved
67.b24.p: The sixty rebels chose Nod as their leader, but they soon lost the support of the system life circuits and fell to the status of mortal beings. At Daligastia's order they began to have children, and their descendants became known as the Nodites, their home as “⟦Q 67:4.2|74:8.8|76:2.9⟧the land of Nod.⟦/Q⟧” Legends of gods coming down to mate with mortals, and much later idolatry, grew from these days. The fate of the sixty is not known; their Adjusters still wait on Jerusem. Yet the great majority of those misled by the rebellion have long since heartily repented, and the authors believe all such sincere penitents will in some way be rehabilitated.
67.b26.p: For almost fifty years after the rebellion Dalamatia was in great confusion. Revolution displaced evolution as the policy of cultural advance, and when radical methods were tried on the outlying peoples, liberty was quickly translated into license. Taught the doctrine of liberty too soon, semisavage tribes swept down on the city and drove the rebel staff northward. Society sank back to its old biologic level.
67.b27.p: One hundred and sixty-two years after the rebellion a tidal wave swept over Dalamatia, and the planetary headquarters sank beneath the sea. By then the renegades who remained there had turned the Father's temple into a shrine to Nog, the false god of light and fire.
67.b29.p: Van's followers withdrew to the highlands west of India and planned the rebuilding of the world. Van placed the administration of human affairs in ten commissions of four each, and when the loyal staff returned to Jerusem, the Amadonites took up these duties. The 144 Amadonites became a biologic leaven that kept supplying leadership for the world through the long dark ages that followed.
67.b30.p: Sustained by the tree of life and the ministry of the Melchizedeks, Van and Amadon lived for over one hundred and fifty thousand years and worked until the coming of Adam. Urantia was governed by a council of twelve Melchizedek receivers, and Van faithfully carried out their policies; within a thousand years of the rebellion he had more than three hundred and fifty advanced groups scattered over the world. Edentia had at once upheld Van's appeal on every point, but the circuits were cut while the ruling was in transit. Only recently was it found, lodged in a relay energy transmitter.
67.b32.p: The personal consequences of willfully rejecting light concern only God and that one creature. But the outward repercussions of sin are collective and touch every being within their range. Fifty thousand years after the planetary administration collapsed, mankind had gained very little over its condition when Caligastia arrived.
67.b33.t: Individual, a matter between God and the creature
Collective, reaching every being within range
Intellectual development, moral growth, social progress
The highest spiritual achievement of anyone who chooses to know God and do his will
67.b34.p: Sin is fatal to personality survival only when it becomes the attitude of the whole being, the choosing of the mind and the willing of the soul. Caligastia rebelled and Adam and Eve defaulted, yet no mortal born since has suffered in his personal spiritual experience because of it. Sin is wholly personal as to moral guilt or spiritual consequences.
67.b35.h: 8. The Human Hero of the Rebellion
67.b36.p: The records of Salvington portray Amadon as the outstanding character of the entire system, for he rejected the flood tides of sedition and never wavered in his devotion to Van. The Melchizedek author recalls the joy he felt on Edentia as day after day the broadcasts told of the steadfastness of this onetime semisavage. For seven long years, the first question asked all the way up to Uversa was always the same:
67.b37.q: “⟦Q 67:8.3⟧What of Amadon of Urantia, does he still stand unmoved?⟦/Q⟧”
67.b38.p: The loyalty of Amadon and his 143 comrades has already done more good in Nebadon and Orvonton than all the evil and sorrow of the Lucifer rebellion can ever outweigh. And it shines a beautiful light on the wisdom of the Father's plan to recruit the Corps of Mortal Finality largely from the common clay of ascending mortals — just such mortals as the impregnable Amadon.
67.b40.p: Paper 67 tells of a rebellion that wrecked a world, and of the loyalty that shone in its ruins. The Prince with the greatest intellect and experience fell into self-exaltation and betrayed his trust; as a result Dalamatia sank into the sea and human progress was long delayed. But Amadon, a man with little intellect and no experience, stood unshaken beside Van for seven years while the whole universe waited for news of him. Sin leaves wide wounds on society and civilization, yet its moral guilt and spiritual consequences are wholly personal. So no one else's sin can stop our choice to know God and do his will.
67.b41.t: Betrayal of trust is the sin that most deeply destroys personality
On a cut-off planet, every being was forced to choose
Not intellect but the union of mind and spirit kept Amadon steadfast
4. The Caligastia One Hundred after Rebellion
Forty were saved; sixty fell to mortal status
Liberty given too soon became license, and the headquarters sank into the sea
Van and the Amadonites kept the flame of civilization alive through the dark ages
Sin's effects spread widely, but its spiritual consequences are wholly personal
8. The Human Hero of the Rebellion
One ordinary mortal's loyalty did more good than all the evil of the rebellion
67.b43.box: Another's sin may throw the world into confusion, but it can never defeat one person's choice to be loyal to God.
68.title: The Dawn of Civilization
68.b0.ask: “Civilization is not born in us — so what first drove mankind to build it, and how has it been carried forward?”
68.b2.p: In the papers before this one we saw the missions of the Planetary Prince and of Adam, and what became of Urantia when they miscarried. With Paper 68 the story turns toward man himself. It begins the account of the long, long struggle by which mankind rose from a status little better than an animal existence to a real, though imperfect, civilization.
68.b3.p: The starting point of this paper is a single sentence: civilization is a racial acquirement; it is not biologically inherent. The higher qualities of civilization — scientific, philosophic, and religious — are not passed on by inheritance, so every child must be reared in a culture and every generation must be educated anew. The co-operative social order began with the Dalamatia teachers, who for three hundred thousand years nurtured mankind in the idea of group activities.
68.b4.p: What, then, drew together primitive men who felt no natural affection for one another? And what keeps a society standing, and what brings it down?
68.b5.q: ⟦Q 68:2.11⟧Self-maintenance builds society; unbridled self-gratification unfailingly destroys civilization.⟦/Q⟧
68.b8.p: Primitive man was not naturally overflowing with brotherly feeling. The early races learned only by sad experience that “⟦Q 68:1.1|79:5.5⟧in union there is strength,⟦/Q⟧” and this lack of natural brotherly attraction still stands in the way of the brotherhood of man. To go about alone without a tribal mark was fatal, so association became the price of survival.
68.b9.p: Society was born not from a mere gathering of numbers but from the organization of intelligent co-operators. Man learns to co-operate first through fear, and later because he discovers that co-operation is most beneficial. The peoples who organized early survived better, and that is why civilization has kept advancing despite man's many blunders. So the modern cry of “⟦Q 68:1.7⟧back to nature,⟦/Q⟧” the paper says, is a delusion — a belief in a golden age that never was.
68.b10.q: ⟦Q 68:1.2⟧Civilization has become man's insurance against violent death, while the premiums are paid by submission to society's numerous law demands.⟦/Q⟧
68.b12.p: The herd instinct alone cannot explain human society as it exists today. Much of man's sociability is acquired, and four great influences brought people together and held them together. History is largely the record of man's food struggle, and food saving was primitive man's first self-discipline.
68.b13.t: First drew people together — an urge shared with the animals
Led to the home, though it was transient and spasmodic
Held people together, since it needs an audience to parade before
Bound society firmly and gave it an extrahuman aspect
68.b14.p: The sex urge alone did not lead men and women to take on the burdens of a home. The early home rested on the restlessness of the male and the devoted mother love of the female, and because of the helpless baby, where woman was came to be regarded as the home. Almost everything of lasting value in civilization has its roots in the family, the first successful peace group. Vanity gave rise to art, ceremony, and games. But today, the paper warns, pleasure-want has replaced hunger-want, and self-maintenance is turning into dangerous self-gratification.
68.b15.t: Together with self-maintenance, the real object of the home and marriage
68.b17.p: If primitive desires produced society, ghost fear held it together. Ordinary fear was physiological — fear of pain or hunger — but ghost fear was a new and sublime sort of terror. The paper names the ghost dream as probably the greatest single factor in the evolution of human society. Animals do not imagine survival after death, so this was one of the earliest differences between the animal mind and the human mind.
68.b18.p: This baseless fear whipped loose groups into better-disciplined ones and prepared men's minds for the later discovery of “⟦Q 68:3.3⟧the fear of the Lord which is the beginning of wisdom.⟦/Q⟧” The fears of evolution are meant to be replaced by the awe for Deity inspired by revelation. Yet hunger, love, vanity, and fear alone cannot bear the strain of human relations; in the end they drive mankind into war. The peace tendency of the human race is not natural; it comes from revealed religion, and above all from the teachings of Jesus, the Prince of Peace.
68.b19.t: Enables society to bear the strain and fosters peace
68.b21.p: All modern social institutions grew out of the primitive customs of our savage ancestors. What habit is to the individual, custom is to the group, and group customs develop into folkways and traditions. The mores were man's first social institution, born of the effort to avoid pain and humiliation while seeking pleasure and power. What fixed them firmly was the belief that the dead would punish the living who scorned their ways of life.
68.b22.p: Before the Dalamatia teachers came, the savage was a slave to the tyranny of usage from morning until night. Yet custom is not wholly evil. The inertia of primitive man served as a biologic safety brake against changes that came too fast, and custom has been the thread of continuity that held civilization together. No civilization has endured which abandoned its mores except by adopting better ones, and not every change was progress; there have been many retrogressions.
68.b23.t: A tyranny of usage with nothing free, spontaneous, or original
Protects against the maladjustment of a too rapidly advancing civilization
Gradual evolution, not radical revolution, keeps civilization alive
68.b25.p: Land is the stage of society; men are the actors. The evolution of the mores always depends on the land-man ratio, and man's land technique plus his standard of living equal the sum of his folkways and mores. The earliest cultures arose along the rivers of the Eastern Hemisphere, and the march of civilization took four great steps.
68.b26.t: Hunger led to food-gathering lines — a primitive nomadic culture
Weapon tools freed man from much of his food slavery
Man lived on the interest of his capital, the increase of his flocks
The domestication of plants — the highest type of material civilization
68.b27.p: The pastoral life gave more leisure but sharply lowered woman's status. Man now got his food from his herds and became independent of woman, and by the close of that era, the paper records, she had become scarcely more than a human animal. Agriculture more than quadrupled the land-man ratio, and the growing of plants ennobles all races. Hunters and herders were warlike, while the farmer is more peace-loving, and even an industrial age cannot survive unless it rests on a sound agricultural basis.
68.b29.p: Man is a creature of the soil, and his basic struggle was, is, and ever shall be for land. The land-man ratio underlies all social civilization. Population varies directly with the land arts and inversely with the standard of living. When land was plentiful, human life was highly valued; when land was scarce, life grew cheap.
68.b30.t: Lower land yield or more people
The struggle is renewed and the worst traits of human nature surface
Better yield, better mechanical arts, fewer people
The better side of human nature develops
They multiply their inhabitants' power for good or evil
Smaller families; excessive luxury becomes suicidal
68.b31.p: The paper calmly records that the early races turned to infanticide and abortion to limit their numbers, and that many clans were virtually exterminated by these practices. Yet very few children were destroyed once they had been suckled — maternal affection was too strong. Finally the paper looks ahead: as war and disease are reduced, population may become the great test of the wisdom of world leadership. The normal man should be fostered, for he is the backbone of civilization.
68.b33.p: Paper 68 shows that civilization is not built into human nature. It began when people, driven by hunger and fear, reluctantly banded together. Vanity and ghost fear held that union in place; custom was both a bondage and the thread that carried civilization forward; and the land-man ratio lay beneath it all. But as the paper keeps insisting, these evolutionary motives alone cannot bring peace. When self-maintenance decays into self-gratification, civilization falls, and mankind's peace comes from revelation and the teachings of Jesus. That is why civilization is an inheritance that must be taught and guarded anew in every generation.
68.b34.t: Not brotherly love but fear and need first drew people together
Hunger, sex, vanity, and fear gathered and held society
Ghost fear bound society, but peace comes from revelation
Custom is both bondage and the thread of continuity
Civilization advanced through collecting, hunting, herding, and farming
The land-man ratio underlies all social civilization
68.b36.box: Civilization is an inheritance that is not passed on by birth; self-maintenance builds society, but unbridled self-gratification brings civilization down.
69.title: Primitive Human Institutions
69.b0.ask: “Out of what fears and needs were today's institutions — industry and trade, capital and property — born, and how should we govern them?”
69.b2.p: In Paper 68 we saw how hunger and fear first drew people together, and how custom hardened into the mores that carried civilization forward. Paper 69 looks one by one at the institutions that grew from those long-accumulated customs. Man rises above his animal ancestors not only in his ability to appreciate humor, art, and religion, but also because he is a toolmaker, a communicator, and an institution builder.
69.b3.p: Social groups that last long always end in institutions, and most of these have saved labor while adding to the group's security. Yet all human institutions are merely the accumulated mores of the past, conserved by taboos and dignified by religion. Such legacies become traditions, and traditions in time become conventions.
69.b4.p: From what needs, then, did industry and trade, capital and private property grow? And what must we understand if we are to govern our institutions rather than be ruled by them?
69.b5.q: ⟦Q 69:1.1⟧Man should control his institutions rather than permit himself to be dominated by these creations of advancing civilization.⟦/Q⟧
69.b8.p: Every human institution serves some social need, yet when overdeveloped it lowers the worth of the individual by overshadowing personality and weakening initiative. That is why man must control his institutions. The paper sorts them into three classes, which are so closely interwoven that they function as a single social mechanism.
69.b9.t: Industry, property, war for gain, the regulative machinery of society
Sex hunger and the maternal instinct
Home, school, education, ethics, religion, marriage customs
Dress and adornment, war for glory, dancing, games
69.b10.p: Two further points are worth remembering: fear, ignorance, and superstition played a prominent part in the early origin of every institution, and civilization has never evolved distinctive institutions of self-gratification.
69.b12.p: Primitive industry grew up slowly as insurance against the terrors of famine; man learned from animals that store food in times of plenty. Poverty is man's natural estate, and wealth is not a natural gift. Association led to organization, and organization to division of labor. What drove the naturally inactive early races into industry was the double demand of the struggle for existence and the rising standard of living.
69.b13.p: Labor, the effort of design, sets man apart from the beast, and the necessity for labor is man's paramount blessing. The Prince's staff all worked, Adam was a gardener, and the Hebrews were the first people to decree that “⟦Q 69:2.5⟧he who does not work shall not eat.⟦/Q⟧” Primitive man, a born gambler, always wanted something for nothing, but magic slowly gave way before foresight, self-denial, and industry.
69.b14.q: ⟦Q 69:2.2⟧Wealth is not a natural gift; it results from labor, knowledge, and organization.⟦/Q⟧
69.b16.p: Division of labor in primitive society was decided first by natural and then by social circumstances, and the paper lists five steps in its early order. The medicine men were the first professional class, freed from physical toil. The smiths, who worked metals, competed with them as magicians; in this first contest between science and religion, religion (superstition) won, and the smiths, driven from the villages, kept the first inns on the outskirts of the settlements.
69.b17.t: Woman became the routine worker; man the hunter and fighter
Old men and cripples made tools and weapons, and later built irrigation works
The medicine men became the first professional class; the smiths their rivals
Conqueror and conquered — the beginning of human slavery
Differences of body and mind favored further divisions
69.b18.p: Then came group specialists: flint flakers, stone masons, smiths, rock salt exporters, and potters. The early traders were women, who acted as intermediaries until a merchant class arose that charged a commission for its services.
69.b20.p: Just as marriage by contract followed marriage by capture, trade by barter followed seizure by raids. The first barter was silent: armed traders left their goods on a neutral spot. Women, as the burden bearers, held the first markets. Goods guarded by a fetish were safe from theft, and the market places later became the first sanctuaries, known in some lands as “⟦Q 69:4.4⟧cities of refuge.⟦/Q⟧”
69.b21.t: Grains of wheat as weights; a fish or a goat as money, later the cow
Born of trade records — the first literature was a salt advertisement
The first tribal treaty concerned the sharing of a salt deposit
Traders carried new ideas and better methods around the world
69.b22.p: Commerce, linked with adventure, led to exploration, discovery, and transportation. By promoting the cross-fertilization of culture, the paper says, commerce has been the great civilizer.
69.b24.p: Capital is labor applied as a renunciation of the present in favor of the future. Food hoarding developed self-control and also created the first problems of capital and labor. The early banker was the valorous man of the tribe who held the group's treasures, so the accumulation of wealth led at once to military organization. The paper names eight basic urges behind the accumulation of capital.
69.b25.t: Storing food against famine and disaster
Saving for the needs of one's posterity
Displaying possessions, such as extra clothing
Lending at one hundred per cent a year; debt slavery
Death presents to the priests, who grew very rich
Buying wives — the traffic in women was a racial disgrace
69.b26.p: Man's technique varies, but his disposition remains quite unchanged: the old custom of giving away property on a holiday to win a great name lives on in today's gifts and philanthropy. The paper records as a fact that, despite the abuses of unfair capitalists, capital is the basis of modern industrial society, and that through capital and invention the present generation enjoys more freedom than any before it.
69.b28.p: Primitive society rose through fire, animals, slaves, and property. Fire building, by a single bound, forever separated man from animal; it is the basic human invention. Fire let man stay on the ground at night, encouraged evening fellowship, and was used as protection against ghosts as well as cold and wild beasts.
69.b29.p: Fire gave man his first way of being altruistic without loss, since he could give live coals to a neighbor without depriving himself. The early home was not a building but the family gathered about the fire. Andon, the discoverer of fire, did not worship it, but many of his descendants treated it as a fetish and drifted into fire worship. Fire led to cooking, which saved vital energy, and it opened the doors to metalwork, steam power, and electricity.
69.b30.t: Guarded the night against cold, beasts, and ghosts
The first means of altruism without loss
The family hearth, which taught watchfulness and dependability
Less energy spent on digestion, more left for social culture
Led on to metalwork, steam power, and electricity
69.b32.p: At first the whole animal world was man's enemy. Man first ate the animals, and later learned to tame them and make them serve him. Domestication began by accident, as hunters surrounded herds to keep them for food, and it advanced through selective breeding once species were found that would reproduce in captivity.
69.b33.p: The dog was the first animal to be domesticated, used for food, hunting, transport, and companionship, and watchdogs made it possible for the whole clan to sleep at night. Its keen sense of smell led to the notion that it could see spirits. But after domestication, coupled with the Caligastia confusion, many tribes treated their women much as they treated their animals. Man's brutal treatment of woman, the paper says, is one of the darkest chapters of human history.
69.b34.h: 8. Slavery as a Factor in Civilization
69.b35.p: Primitive man never hesitated to enslave his fellows, and woman was the first slave, a family slave. In earlier times captives were eaten, tortured, or sacrificed, so slavery was a great advancement over massacre and cannibalism. The herders were the first capitalists, living on the increase of their flocks; when they began forcing male prisoners to till the soil, serfdom began.
69.b36.p: Slavery was the bridge over which society passed from chaos and indolence to order, and it gave rise to the beginnings of government. Yet the paper is equally clear that it was oppressive, and that it soon attacks society from within as the gravest of destructive social maladies. Modern machinery has made the slave obsolete, though today thousands let ambition enslave them to debt.
69.b37.t: Man came up from savagery by way of fire, animals, and slavery
Discarding slaves and animals, he reaches back to fire — the inorganic world
Universal freedom, yet idleness should never be tolerated
69.b39.p: Primitive society was virtually communal. Its communism was not a theory but a simple, practical adjustment that prevented pauperism and begging, yet it rewarded idleness and stifled industry and ambition. It gave way to a higher social order because it ran against four strong human tendencies.
69.b40.t: Man wants to leave his goods to his children — there was no inheritance
Man wanted property for the next life — hence burying belongings with the dead
The worker was made slave to the idler
Successful individuals secretly hoarded to escape the idlers
69.b41.p: Private property began with things thought to carry the owner's personality: what he had touched, the place where his blood was shed, his sleeping space, his fire site, his well. Agriculture was the genesis of the private ownership of land. The right to property is not absolute but purely social; even so, government, law, civil rights, and peace as modern peoples enjoy them have all grown up around private property. The present order is not sacred and may be changed, but the paper urges care.
69.b42.q: ⟦Q 69:9.18⟧Make certain that when you change the social order you change for the better. Do not be persuaded to experiment with the discarded formulas of your forefathers. Go forward, not backward!⟦/Q⟧
69.b44.p: Paper 69 shows that the institutions we take for granted — industry and trade, capital and private property — all grew little by little out of hunger and fear, vanity and superstition. Having climbed out of savagery by way of fire, animals, and slaves, mankind now seeks new power in machines and the elements of nature. The paper says no institution is sacred, yet it urges us not to return to formulas our ancestors discarded, but to move forward slowly and for the better. Institutions arose to serve man, so man should be their master, not their servant.
69.b45.t: Section
Key message
1. Basic Human Institutions
Institutions of self-maintenance, self-perpetuation, and self-gratification are interwoven
2. The Dawn of Industry
Wealth is not inborn; it comes from labor, knowledge, and organization
3. The Specialization of Labor
Work was divided by sex, age, religion, conquest, and talent
4. The Beginnings of Trade
Silent barter gave rise to writing and the exchange of culture
5. The Beginnings of Capital
Capital is labor that gives up the present for the future
6. Fire in Relation to Civilization
Fire was the first great civilizer that set man apart from the animal
7. The Utilization of Animals
Animals that were once enemies were tamed into man's helpers
8. Slavery as a Factor in Civilization
Slavery, a school of oppression, is passing before the machine
9. Private Property
Property rights are social; change slowly and for the better
69.b47.box: Every institution grew out of need and fear, so man must govern his institutions rather than be ruled by them, and move them forward for the better.
70.title: The Evolution of Human Government
70.b0.ask: “For a race whose natural state was fighting, how did mankind move from war to courts, and from chiefs to representative government, slowly learning peace?”
70.b2.p: In Paper 69 we saw how institutions such as industry, capital, and private property grew out of need and fear. Paper 70 takes up the next step. No sooner had man partly solved the problem of making a living than he faced the task of regulating human contacts: industry demanded law and order, and private property necessitated government.
70.b3.p: On an evolutionary world antagonisms are natural, and peace is secured only by some system of social regulation. Government was never designed by anyone; it is an unconscious development that evolves by trial and error. The misery of anarchy and the pressure of the struggle for existence drove mankind along the road to civilization.
70.b4.p: How, then, did quarrelsome primitive men learn to submit to authority? Where did rights, justice, and law come from? And what kind of government should a free people build?
70.b5.q: ⟦Q 70:1.1⟧War is the natural state and heritage of evolving man; peace is the social yardstick measuring civilization's advancement.⟦/Q⟧
70.b8.p: Violence is the law of nature and hostility the automatic reaction of nature's children; war is simply these same activities carried on collectively. Whenever civilization comes under strain, there is a quick and ruinous return to these early methods. War is an animal reaction to misunderstanding and irritation, while peace attends the civilized solution of problems. The Andonites were early taught the golden rule; they settled disputes by beating a tree with a stick or by public contests of ridicule.
70.b9.p: As groups formed, peace within the tribe increased, but at the expense of peace between tribes, and early man thought it a virtue to shed alien blood. The paper lists seven early causes of war.
70.b10.t: Food raids — scarcity of land has always brought on war
Stealing women to relieve a shortage of domestic help
The desire to exhibit tribal prowess
The need for recruits for the labor ranks
Retaliation on a tribe blamed for a tribesman's death
To the young men of early times, war was sport
The desire to make converts to the cult
70.b11.p: The old tribes waged cruel wars at the supposed bidding of their gods, but the paper makes it clear that such atrocities are not instigated by Deity; man merely places the responsibility on his gods. Little by little, war was refined: prisoners were taken, women and noncombatants were spared, wars were formally declared, and holy places and the right of asylum were respected.
70.b13.p: War once brought about social changes that would otherwise have taken ten thousand years, but the price was a temporary return to savagery. War is strong medicine, very costly and most dangerous; it sometimes kills the patient. The paper explains that war had value for past civilizations: it imposed discipline and co-operation, rewarded courage, solidified nationalism, and dissolved the illusion of primitive equality.
70.b14.t: Modern transport and communication do it better
These are now the aims of modern industry
Ambition and invention do it better
Supported the idea of a God of battles
Modern man has been told that God is love
70.b15.p: As bloodletting gave way to better remedies, so war must give way to better methods for curing the ills of nations. If industrialism is to triumph over militarism, it must avoid six dangers: materialism, the worship of wealth-power, luxury, indolence, racial softness, and standardized industrial slavery. The paper does not glorify war; it asks us to understand what war has done so that we can provide peaceful substitutes.
70.b16.q: ⟦Q 70:2.19⟧Do not make the mistake of glorifying war; rather discern what it has done for society so that you may the more accurately visualize what its substitutes must provide in order to continue the advancement of civilization.⟦/Q⟧
70.b18.p: In the most primitive society the horde was everything, but the family took over child rearing while clans and tribes became the social units. Real government appeared only when groups larger than the family began to form. War forced tribal organization on the clans, but it was commerce and trade that held these groups together with some degree of internal peace. The peace of Urantia, the paper says, will be promoted far more by international trade organizations than by sentimental peace planning, and the gain motive becomes a mighty civilizer when it is enlarged by the desire to serve.
70.b19.t: Drinking each other's blood — later saliva, then wine
A dish broken in half and shared; guests paid with tales of travel
The first peace treaties — envoys sucked each other's blood and declared peace
Marriages between chiefs' families sealed the peace
70.b21.p: The first peace group was the family, then the clan, the tribe, the nation, and finally the modern territorial state. That peace groups have grown beyond blood ties to embrace whole nations is most encouraging. The clans were blood-tie groups within the tribe, held together by six common interests.
70.b22.t: Tracing origin back to a common ancestor
Allegiance to a common religious totem
70.b23.p: Clan peace chiefs usually ruled through the mother line, tribal war chiefs through the father line. The clans served well in local self-government, but they greatly delayed the growth of large and strong nations.
70.b25.p: Civil government is a product of gradual evolution, just like marriage, industry, and religion. The first real governing body was the council of the elders, made up of capable old men, and within it lay the seeds of all three functions of government.
70.b26.t: When it set new social usages
70.b27.p: But mankind learned that neither peace nor war can be run by a debating society, and war has always been a kingmaker. War chiefs gradually ruled even in times of peace, while peace chiefs, medicine men, and priests also acted as rulers. So the executive branch arose, and the councils remained as advisory bodies, forerunners of the later legislative and judicial branches.
70.b29.p: Effective state rule came only with a chief who held full executive authority. Man found that effective government could be had only by conferring power on a personality, not by endowing an idea. Hereditary kingship avoided the anarchy that had followed a king's death, and kings gradually became sacred fetish personalities who were greatly feared.
70.b30.p: The representative chosen to stand in for a secluded fetish king was the origin of the prime minister, and as a food administrator and other officers followed, executive authority became depersonalized. Even the most despotic tyrant was checked by the fear of assassination, by the medicine men and priests, by the landowning aristocracy, and by clans and tribes that would rise up against him.
70.b32.p: Blood kinship formed the first social groups, and the tribe created by intermarriage was the first true political body. The next step was the rise of religious cults and political clubs, which first appeared as secret societies. They kept their secrecy for four reasons.
70.b33.t: Of displeasing the rulers by violating some taboo
To practice the religious rites of a minority
To preserve valuable “spirit” or trade secrets
To enjoy some special charm or magic
70.b34.p: The men's societies took boys away from their parents at puberty, taught them sex control, and impressed on them that they must leave other men's wives alone; later women's societies appeared as well. Secret societies gave rise to the first schools, spies, secret police, and political parties, and they kept unscrupulous kings on the anxious seat. In time they grew into the first charitable organizations, forerunners of the churches, and the first international fraternities.
70.b36.p: The mental and physical inequality of human beings ensures that social classes will appear. The only worlds without social strata are the most primitive and the most advanced; a world settled in light and life has largely erased the divisions of the intermediate stages. The paper gives ten reasons why classes form.
70.b37.t: Sex, age, and kinship to the chief
Professional classes, skilled and unskilled workers
70.b38.p: Flexible classes are necessary to an evolving civilization, but when class hardens into caste, stability is bought at the cost of personal initiative and co-operation. The paper names three means by which classes may eventually be dissolved — biologic improvement of the racial stocks, the education that such improvement makes possible, and the religious quickening of brotherhood — and says these will bear their true fruit only in the distant future. Religion is the mighty lever that lifts civilization, but it needs the fulcrum of a sound and normal mind.
70.b40.p: Nature confers no rights on man, only life and a world in which to live it. Society's prime gift to man is security. Gradually society asserted its rights, and the paper lists ten that are recognized today.
70.b41.t: Prevention of personal violence and social disorder
So that all other activities may be spiritually motivated
70.b42.p: Human rights are not natural but entirely social; they are the “⟦Q 70:9.13⟧rules of the game⟦/Q⟧” of ever-changing human competition. The paper says that equality is the child of civilization, not of nature. Society cannot offer equal rights to all, but it can promise to administer the varying rights of each with fairness and equity. Its duty is to give everyone a fair opportunity for self-maintenance, self-perpetuation, and some self-gratification, the sum of which is human happiness.
70.b44.p: In nature, justice is a fiction; nature offers only the inevitable conformity of results to causes. When someone died, primitive man asked not what killed him, but who, so motives were ignored and only the injury was judged. Medicine men and priests tried crimes by ordeals of poison, fire, and pain. Of one such ordeal preserved in scripture, a test for marital guilt, the paper says plainly that no divine being ever gave mortal man such unfair instructions.
70.b45.t: An eye for an eye, a life for a life
The belief that one would return as a ghost to punish an enemy
Damages paid in women or cattle — the first public revenue
Revenge taken from private and kin groups and given to the state
70.b46.p: The administration of true justice dates from the taking of revenge from private and kin groups and lodging it in the hands of the state. It was learned that certainty and swiftness of punishment deter crime better than severity, and that when society fails to punish crime, group anger breaks out as lynch law.
70.b48.p: Mores are laws in the making; once long established, they crystallize into precise laws. Law is always at first negative and prohibitive, as in “⟦Q 70:11.2|66:7.12|93:4.10⟧you shall not kill,⟦/Q⟧” but it becomes more positive and directive as civilization advances. Self-interest established the taboo on killing, society made it a tradition, and religion consecrated it as moral law, together making human life safer. Law is a codified record of long human experience, public opinion crystallized and legalized.
70.b49.t: To the elders, and later to the courts
70.b50.p: The first courts were regulated fistic encounters, with the judge as mere referee; only later did verbal argument replace physical blows. Primitive justice aimed less at fairness than at preventing disorder. Yet the status of any civilization may be accurately judged by the thoroughness and equity of its courts and the integrity of its judges.
70.b52.p: The great struggle in the evolution of government has concerned the concentration of power. The universe administrators have learned from experience that evolutionary peoples are best governed by representative government with a proper balance of power among the executive, legislative, and judicial branches. In barbaric times war gave the victory to the dictator, but the councils of elders survived as advisory bodies and later became legislatures and supreme courts.
70.b53.p: The paper declares that the mortals of Urantia are entitled to liberty: they should adopt their own constitutions and choose their most competent and worthy fellows as leaders and judges. If they would keep their freedom, they must interpret their charter wisely, intelligently, and fearlessly so as to prevent twelve dangers.
70.b54.t: Unwarranted power seized by the executive or legislature
The schemes of ignorant and superstitious agitators
Enslavement of the citizenry by taxation
Failure of social and economic fairness
The union of church and state
70.b55.q: ⟦Q 70:12.20⟧While there is a divine and ideal form of government, such cannot be revealed but must be slowly and laboriously discovered by the men and women of each planet throughout the universes of time and space.⟦/Q⟧
70.b57.p: Paper 70 does not hide the fact that fighting was man's natural state. Upon that foundation mankind passed through councils of elders and kings, secret societies and courts, slowly learning to submit to authority, to hand revenge over to the state, and to argue with words instead of fists. Neither rights nor justice were given by nature; they are rules of the game that society set up after long experience. The paper urges us not to glorify war but to find peaceful ways to do what war once did, and to discover and keep a representative government with a balance of power. An ideal government is not handed down from above; people must work hard to find it for themselves.
70.b58.t: War is the natural state; peace is the measure of civilization
Do not glorify war; find its peaceful substitutes
Trade and bonding rites kept peace within the tribe
Peace groups widened from the family to the nation
The council of elders held executive, legislative, and judicial powers
Effective rule began by conferring power on a personality
Secret societies gave rise to schools, parties, and charities
Flexible classes are needed, but hardened castes do harm
Rights are not inborn; they are society's rules of the game
True justice begins when revenge is handed to the state
Law moved from prohibition to direction, from fists to words
People must discover balanced representative government for themselves
70.b60.box: Peace is not inborn; mankind builds civilization by laboriously discovering substitutes for war and a balanced representative government.
